01.note: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi were standing before their teacher Rav after a lesson and disagreed about what he had said. Each swore an oath that Rav had said it his way. When they asked Rav, he agreed with one of them. The other asked, "Did I then take a false oath?" Rav answered, "Your heart compelled you."
01.why: A teaching about oaths says that someone forced by circumstances beyond his control is not liable to bring an offering for a broken oath. The Gemara asks what such circumstances look like, and answers with this case of a man who swore sincerely but was mistaken.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A student of Rav who swore an oath about what Rav had said.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: A student of Rav who swore the opposite oath about what Rav had said.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Their teacher, who settled what he had said and reassured the one who had sworn wrongly.

terms.meaning: A solemn statement made in God's name. Swearing falsely is a serious sin, and in some cases the one who did it must bring an offering at the Temple to atone.

02.note: The wife of Rav Huna had a case before the judge Rav Nahman. He was caught in a bind: if he stood up for her, as the wife of a Torah scholar deserves, the other side might feel he favored her and hold back their claims; if he did not stand, he would fail to honor her. So he told his attendant to go outside, make a duck fly up and throw it at him, so that he would have to stand up anyway.
02.why: The Gemara is discussing who must stand and who may sit in court, and the Torah scholar's dignity in a trial. Right after this, it asks how Rav Nahman could stand at all when judges should sit while giving a verdict.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge hearing the case, who found a way to stand for the woman without seeming biased.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Torah scholar; his wife was a litigant in the case.

terms.meaning: Literally a 'fellow': someone devoted to careful observance of the commandments. The principle quoted is that the wife of a haver is honored as he is.
One of the two sides in a court case.

03.note: Rav bar Sherevya, a Torah scholar, had a case before Rav Pappa against an ordinary unlearned man. Rav Pappa seated them both. A court officer came, kicked the unlearned man and made him stand up, and Rav Pappa did not tell him to sit down again. The Gemara asks how he could allow it, since the man might now feel too intimidated to press his claims. Rav Pappa reasoned that the man would think: the judge seated me; it is only the officer who has it in for me.
03.why: Rabba bar Rav Huna has just ruled that when a scholar and an unlearned man go to court, both are told to sit, and if the unlearned man stands out of respect that is no problem. This case shows the ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav bar Sherevya
people.about: A Torah scholar who had a court case before Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge, who seated both sides and let the officer's action stand.

terms.meaning: Literally 'people of the land': an ordinary person without Torah learning, as opposed to a Torah scholar.
A court officer who carried out the judges' orders and kept order in the courtroom.

04.note: A man snatched a silver ingot from another. The victim came before Rabbi Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting there, and brought one witness who saw the snatching. The accused said, "Yes, I snatched it, but I snatched what was mine." Rabbi Ami was stuck: one witness is not enough to make him pay, but he cannot be let off either, and having admitted to snatching he counts as a robber who cannot be trusted to swear. Rabbi Abba answered that he is someone who must take an oath but cannot, and such a person pays.
04.why: The Gemara is asking when a single witness who falsely denies what he knows is liable for a false oath of testimony. Abaye says all agree in a case like this one, because here one witness's testimony would make the defendant pay.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The judge before whom the case came.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rabbi Ami, who gave the ruling that settled the case.

terms.meaning: Jewish law needs two witnesses to make someone pay. A single witness cannot do that, but he can force the defendant to swear an oath denying the claim.

terms.term: obligated to take an oath but unable to
terms.meaning: A rule that someone who must swear to clear himself, but is not allowed to swear (for example because he is presumed a thief), has to pay instead.

05.note: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah swore that he had seen a man chase another into a ruin. He ran after them and found the man with a sword in his hand, blood dripping, and the victim in his death throes. He said, "Wicked one, who killed this man? Either I did or you did. But what can I do? Your blood is not in my hands, since the Torah requires two witnesses to put a man to death. The Omnipresent will exact payment from you." The Sages said they had not moved from there before a snake bit the killer and he died.
05.why: Rav Pappa is asking whether testimony based on knowledge without seeing the act can exist in capital cases. Rabbi Aha holds that circumstantial evidence counts, and this case is the example of knowing a man killed without seeing it.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Shatah
people.about: The Sage who saw the aftermath of the killing and tells the story under oath.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
A name for God, meaning the One who is everywhere.

terms.term: I will not see the consolation
terms.meaning: A form of oath: may I not live to see the comfort and redemption of Israel if what I say is untrue.

06.note: A man told another, "I lent you a hundred dinars beside this column." The other answered, "I never passed beside this column." Two witnesses came and said they had seen him urinate beside that very column. Reish Lakish ruled that he is now presumed to be a man who denies the truth.
06.why: Just before, Rav Yehuda asked whether witnesses who saw money being counted out from outside can testify about the loan. The Gemara brings a similar case of witnesses who undercut a denial, and Rav Nahman then rejects Reish Lakish's ruling as fit only for a Persian court.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the man who denied passing the column is presumed a liar.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; a hundred dinars was a sizable loan.
Once a person is shown to have lied in a case, the court no longer believes his claims in that case.

07.note: In another version of the case, a man told another, "I lent you a hundred dinars beside this column." The other answered, "I never in my life passed beside this column." Witnesses came and said they had seen him urinate beside that column. Rav Nahman ruled that he is now presumed to be a man who denies the truth.
07.why: In the first version Rav Nahman objected because the man only denied passing the column in connection with the loan. Here he said "never," so Rav Nahman accepts the ruling; Rava then objects that people do not remember things they have no reason to.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: In this version, the Sage who ruled that the man is presumed a liar.

terms.meaning: Once a person is shown to have lied in a case, the court no longer believes his claims in that case.

08.note: A man told another, "Give me the six hundred dinars you owe me." The other answered, "Didn't I pay you with a hundred kav of gallnuts worth six dinars a kav?" The lender replied, "Weren't they worth only four a kav?" Two witnesses came and said yes, they were worth four. Rava ruled that the borrower is now presumed to be a man who denies the truth. Rami bar Hama objected that Rava himself had said people forget things they have no reason to remember. Rava answered that people do remember the market price.
08.why: This is one of a series of cases about when a debtor caught in a false claim loses credibility. Rava has just said a debtor wrongly naming witnesses to a repayment may simply have forgotten; this case shows where he draws the line.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the borrower is presumed a liar.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: A Sage who challenged Rava with his own earlier ruling.

terms.meaning: A measure of volume used for dry goods.
Round growths on oak trees, used for tanning leather and making ink, and traded as a commodity.
Once a person is shown to have lied in a case, the court no longer believes his claims in that case.

09.note: A borrower told his lender, "I will believe you any time you tell me I have not repaid you." He then went and repaid the debt in front of witnesses, and the lender later said he had not been paid. Abaye and Rava both said the lender is believed, since the borrower had agreed to trust him. Rav Pappa objected: he trusted him more than himself, but did he trust him more than witnesses?
09.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a lender's claim that a payment went to some other debt is believed. This case turns to a borrower who gave his lender advance credibility, and the next cases test how far such a promise reaches.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who, with Rava, ruled that the lender is believed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who, with Abaye, ruled that the lender is believed.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who objected that the borrower never meant to trust the lender over witnesses.

10.note: A borrower told his lender he would believe him any time he said the debt had not been repaid, then repaid it in front of witnesses. Abaye and Rava said the lender is believed; Rav Pappa asked whether the borrower meant to trust him even over witnesses. In a second case, a borrower said he would believe the lender as if he were two witnesses, then repaid in front of three. Rav Pappa said the lender was trusted like two, not like three. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua objected: in testimony a hundred witnesses are like two and two are like a hundred. The second case is then told again in another version, with the same ruling.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a lender is believed that a payment went to some other debt. These cases ask how far a borrower's promise to trust his lender reaches against witnesses to a repayment.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who, with Rava, ruled that the lender is believed.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who, with Abaye, ruled that the lender is believed.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who limited how far the borrower's promise of trust reaches.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who objected that in testimony, numbers beyond two make no difference.

terms.meaning: The rule that where people give opinions, such as estimating a value, the larger group is followed. Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says this does not apply to witnesses.

10.flag: The span joins several short cases and a repeated second version of the same case; the first case also appears on its own as a separate story.

11.note: A man snatched a piece of metal from another. The victim came before Rav Ami, with Rabbi Abba sitting there, and brought one witness who saw the snatching. The accused said, "Yes, I snatched it, but I snatched what was mine." Rabbi Ami asked how to judge it: one witness is not enough to make him pay, he cannot be let off since there is a witness, and he cannot be told to swear because by admitting the snatching he counts as a robber. Rabbi Abba answered that he is someone who must take an oath but cannot, and such a person pays.
11.why: The Gemara is asking what Rabbi Yosei meant when he said that an oath nobody can take "returns to its place." Rav Pappa says the Sages of the Land of Israel meant Rabbi Abba, and this case shows Rabbi Abba holding that the defendant who cannot swear must pay.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: The judge before whom the case came (called Rav Ami at first in the English).

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage sitting with Rabbi Ami, who gave the ruling that settled the case.

terms.meaning: Jewish law needs two witnesses to make someone pay. A single witness cannot do that, but he can force the defendant to swear an oath denying the claim.

terms.term: obligated to take an oath but unable to
terms.meaning: A rule that someone who must swear to clear himself, but is not allowed to swear (for example because he is presumed a thief), has to pay instead.

12.note: In the future, God holds up a Torah scroll and invites whoever studied it to take a reward. Rome enters first and says it built markets and bathhouses and amassed silver and gold, all so the Jewish people could study Torah. God calls them fools: the markets were for prostitutes, the bathhouses for their own pleasure, and the silver and gold are His. They leave disappointed. Persia comes next, claiming its bridges, conquered cities and wars were for Israel; God answers that the bridges were for tolls, the cities for forced labor, and the wars were His. Every nation tries in turn. They then plead that they would have accepted the Torah had God held a mountain over them as He did over Israel. God answers: you accepted seven commandments, so where did you keep them?
12.why: The Gemara is expounding a verse from Isaiah about the nations gathering for judgment: "Who among them can declare this?" This scene acts out the verse line by line, with "this" read as the Torah.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who judges the nations and answers each of their claims.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage quoted that God offered the Torah to every nation, and none accepted it but Israel.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage quoted that when a king and a community are judged, the king goes first.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage quoted that the bear in Daniel's vision is Persia.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Hama
people.about: A Sage quoted that God held Mount Sinai over Israel like a basin.

terms.meaning: Seven basic commandments, such as not to murder or steal, that the Sages taught apply to all humanity, the descendants of Noah.
Forced labor that a ruler could demand of the people of a conquered place.

terms.term: overturned the mountain like a basin
terms.meaning: A teaching that at Sinai God held the mountain over Israel like an upturned tub and told them to accept the Torah or be buried there.

13.note: Rabbi Abbahu praised Rav Safra to the heretics as a great man, and because of that they let him off his taxes for thirteen years. One day they met Rav Safra and asked him about a verse in Amos: if God loves Israel, why does He punish them for all their sins? Does one who is angry take it out on the one he loves? Rav Safra was silent. They threw a scarf around his neck and tormented him. Rabbi Abbahu came upon them and explained that he had praised Rav Safra's learning in the Oral Law, not in the Bible; Sages in the Land of Israel study verses closely because they must debate the heretics. When they asked him for the answer, he gave a parable: a man who lends to a friend and to an enemy collects from the friend little by little, and from the enemy all at once.
13.why: The Gemara has been explaining that God punishes Israel for each sin in small portions so as not to destroy them all at once, and that their sufferings in this world are meant for their good. Rabbi Abbahu's parable makes the same point.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage who praised Rav Safra to the heretics, then rescued him and answered their question.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Sage whose tax was remitted on Rabbi Abbahu's word, and who could not answer the heretics about the verse.

terms.meaning: The English translation's word for people who argued with the Sages about the meaning of Scripture.
The early Sages whose teachings make up the Mishna and related works. Rabbi Abbahu means Rav Safra is an expert in their oral teachings.
A short illustrative tale, often about a king or an ordinary person, used to explain a teaching.

14.note: A heretic kept tormenting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi with challenges about verses. One day Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi took a rooster, set it between the legs of his bed and watched it, planning to curse the heretic at the exact moment when God is angry. When that moment came, he fell asleep. He concluded that it is not proper to do such a thing, since Scripture says God's mercies are over all His works and that punishing even the righteous is not good.
14.why: Abaye has just taught that God is angry for a moment within the first three hours of the day, and that the sign is a rooster's comb turning fully white. The story shows a Sage trying to use that sign.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: A Sage harassed by a heretic, who tried to curse him at the moment of God's anger.

terms.meaning: The English translation's word for someone who argued with the Sages about the meaning of Scripture.
The Gemara teaches that God's anger lasts only an instant each day; a curse spoken then was thought to take effect.

15.note: A heretic sent a Caesarean dinar, a Roman coin, to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia on the day of his festival. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia asked Reish Lakish, who was sitting before him, what to do: if he took it, the man would go and give thanks to his idol; if he refused, the man would bear him a grudge. Reish Lakish said to take it and throw it into a pit in front of him. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia objected that this would make the grudge even worse. Reish Lakish explained that he meant to do it in an offhand way, as if it slipped from his hand.
15.why: The Mishna forbids doing business with idol worshippers around their festivals, and the Gemara explains that the worry is the gentile will thank his idol for his success. This gift on the festival day is a case of that worry in real life.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: A Sage who received the coin and asked what to do with it.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage sitting before Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, who told him how to get rid of it.

terms.meaning: The English translation's word here for a non-Jew who worshipped idols and kept their festivals.
A Roman coin, probably one minted with the emperor's image.

16.note: Rav Dimi reported that the Romans fought thirty-two battles against the Greeks and could not beat them until they made an alliance with the Jewish people. Their terms: if the kings come from us, the governors come from you, and the reverse. The Romans then sent the Greeks a riddle to settle the matter by judgment. Which should be set beneath which: a pearl or a precious stone? The Greeks answered that the pearl goes under the precious stone, the precious stone under the onyx, and the onyx under the Torah scroll. The Romans replied: then we have the Torah scroll, and Israel is with us. They forced the Greeks to submit. For twenty-six years the Romans kept faith with the Jewish people, and after that they subjugated them.
16.why: The Mishna lists Kratesis among Roman festivals, and Rav Yosef says Rome seized an empire twice, once in the days of the Greeks. Rav Dimi's account explains that earlier conquest.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel and reported this account.

terms.meaning: A Roman festival listed in the Mishna, which the Gemara links to the day Rome seized control of an empire.
Governors: officials who ruled provinces under the king.
The translation's word here for an especially valuable precious stone.

17.note: The wicked kingdom of Rome decreed that anyone who ordained judges would be killed, anyone ordained would be killed, the city where it happened would be destroyed, and its surrounding area uprooted. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava went and sat between two large mountains and two large cities, between Usha and Shefaram, and ordained five Elders there: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua; Rav Avya adds Rabbi Nehemya. When enemies found them, he told them, "My sons, run!" They asked what would become of him. He said he was lying before them like a stone that cannot be turned over. It was said that the soldiers did not leave until they had driven three hundred iron spears into his body and made it like a sieve.
17.why: Rav says that without Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava the laws of fines would have been lost, and the Gemara asks how, since one could just study them. It answers that only ordained judges can rule on fines, and this story shows how he kept ordination alive against Rome's decree.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
people.about: A Sage who ordained new judges in defiance of the Roman decree and was killed for it.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: One of the five Elders he ordained.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua
people.about: One of the five Elders he ordained.

people.name: Rav Avya
people.about: A Sage who adds that Rabbi Nehemya was also ordained.

terms.meaning: The formal appointment of a Sage as a judge, passed from teacher to student. Only ordained judges could rule in certain cases, such as fines.
Penalties set by the Torah at a fixed amount, beyond simple repayment for damage. Only ordained judges could impose them.
The limit around a town beyond which one may not walk on the Sabbath. Sitting between two of them meant being in no town's area.

18.note: Antoninus, a Roman ruler, told Rabbi (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) that he wanted his son Asveirus to rule after him and Tiberias to be freed from taxes, but the Senate would grant only one request. Rabbi set one man on another's shoulders, put a dove in the top man's hands, and told the bottom man to tell the top one to let it fly. Antoninus understood: ask the Senate to make Asveirus king, and have Asveirus free Tiberias. Antoninus also said important Romans were upsetting him. Rabbi took him into his garden and each day pulled up one radish before him. Antoninus understood: kill them one by one, and do not provoke them all at once. Rabbi did not speak openly for fear the Romans would hear, nor in a whisper, since a bird of the air carries the voice.
18.why: The Gemara has said the Romans did not make a king's son king, then explains that they did when the king asked, as with Asveirus son of Antoninus. This story shows how that came about.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman ruler and friend of Rabbi, who asked his advice in secret.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the leading Sage, who answered Antoninus with silent signs.

people.name: Asveirus
people.about: Antoninus's son, whom he wanted to succeed him.

terms.meaning: A word the translation renders as a city released from paying taxes.

19.note: Antoninus had a tunnel running from his house to the house of Rabbi. Each day he brought two servants, killed one at Rabbi's door and the other at his own, so no one would know of his visits. He told Rabbi to let no one be with him when he came. One day he found Rabbi Hanina bar Hama sitting there. Rabbi said this was no ordinary human being. Antoninus told Rabbi Hanina to go and wake the servant sleeping at the entrance. Rabbi Hanina found the servant had been killed. Not wanting to bring bad news, nor to slight the king by ignoring him, he prayed for mercy, revived the servant and sent him in. Antoninus said: I know even the least of you can revive the dead, but still let no one be with you when I come.
19.why: This is one of a run of stories about the secret friendship between Antoninus and Rabbi, which the Gemara tells after explaining how Antoninus's son came to rule.

people.name: Antoninus
people.about: A Roman ruler who visited Rabbi in secret.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the leading Sage, Antoninus's friend.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama
people.about: A Sage found with Rabbi, who revived the dead servant through prayer.

20.note: A teaching says a verse about Edom in the netherworld leaves out Antoninus son of Asveirus and the Roman officer Ketia bar Shalom. An emperor who hated the Jews asked his nobles whether a man with a sore on his foot should cut it off and live. They said yes. Ketia objected that the Jews cannot all be destroyed, since the world cannot exist without them, and that Rome would be called the severed kingdom. The emperor said he spoke well, but whoever defeats the king is thrown into a house of ashes. As he was led away, a noblewoman said, "Woe to the ship that sails without paying the tax." Ketia cut off his foreskin and said he had paid, and left his property to Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues. A Divine Voice declared him destined for the World-to-Come, and Rabbi wept.
20.why: Antoninus asked Rabbi whether verses about Edom, read as Rome, exclude him from the World-to-Come. The Gemara backs Rabbi's answer with a teaching that two Romans are excepted, and explains who the second one was.

people.name: Ketia bar Shalom
people.about: A Roman officer who argued against destroying the Jews and was put to death for it.

people.name: Antoninus son of Asveirus
people.about: A Roman ruler the teaching says is excepted from the verse about Edom.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage to whom Ketia left his property, and who taught how it should be divided.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who wept on hearing that Ketia had earned the World-to-Come.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
A heavenly voice that the Sages describe announcing God's judgment.
The life of reward after this world.
The noblewoman's riddle: Ketia had not been circumcised. By cutting off his foreskin he became Jewish before he died.
